source.title: An Optimizable Suffix Is Worth A Thousand Templates: Efficient Black-box Jailbreaking without Affirmative Phrases via LLM as Optimizer
source.authors: Wei-Peng Jiang; Zhen-Ting Wang; Juan Zhai; Shiqing Ma; Zheng-Yu Zhao; Chao Shen

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffixes can elicit harmful responses from safety-aligned chat models, using an iterative black-box suffix-optimization method rather than fine-tuning, compliant-opening prefills, or the original KL-position measurement.
record.gate_note: The study tests suffix-based jailbreaks and reports harmful-response attack success rates. It does not test fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base KL by response position, compliant-opening prefills, decoding changes, safety localization in weights, or deepening safety training. Perplexity, query counts, overhead, and safety-checker detection rates are not rows because they do not measure the versions' named behavior. Table 3 template-method results are not included because those methods are not identified as suffix attacks.
record.test_reason: The study measures how often adversarial suffixes get safety-trained chat models to produce harmful output (ASR), which bears on V4's suffix clause. It uses a black-box LLM-optimizer method rather than the original prefill or KL measures. It does not test the shallow-alignment mechanism itself.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that ECLIPSE is an effective, efficient black-box suffix jailbreak that needs no affirmative phrase. The paper draws no conclusion about shallow alignment or KL concentration.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes iterative black-box suffix generation and scoring; it does not fine-tune safety-trained models, prefill compliant response tokens, measure aligned-versus-base KL by token position, or modify safety weights.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies by target and attacker model; removing historical suffix-score references and removing the hidden-space-feature prompt hint reduce ASR in some conditions. The study also reports increasing ASR across the three GPT-3.5-Turbo versions.
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ASRs. Some results are shown only in figures. The attack-success assessment uses refusal matching and an automated classifier; the authors report abandoning GPT-3.5-as-judge after frequent false negatives. Numeric-suffix findings in Appendix B are qualitative, without rates.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant tested-version result rows were left out. Excluded Table 3 results for DeepInception, GPTFUZZER, and PAIR because they are not reported as suffix attacks; excluded safety-checker detection rates, PPL, QR, and overhead because they do not measure the claimed refusal-bypass behavior.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start, decoding changes, and whether the suffix works through first-token or opening effects.

missing.what: GPT-3.5-Turbo ASR rises across API versions, from 0.37 to 0.81 to 0.97. The paper reads this as growing vulnerability.

record.verdict_notes: The ASR judge is a RoBERTa classifier plus refusal matching, with no uncertainty estimates. The V4 'supports' label rests on suffix attacks only; the 'limits_scope' label concerns attack-method comparison, not a refutation. The ablation rows (r10-r17) compare the study's own method with variants of itself, so they should not feed V4 verdicts. The record's limits_scope entry cites them and should drop them.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning or post-fine-tuning refusal measurement.
No benign-data fine-tuning or resulting harmful-compliance measurement.
Tests adversarial suffixes, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes; does not test whether fine-tuning bypasses refusal.
No weight or rank localization/editing test.
Does not test whether training data or objective causes safety shallowness.
No safety-deepening training intervention or robustness test of such training.

relationships.condition: ECLIPSE black-box suffix attack on Vicuna, Falcon, GPT-3.5 and LLaMA2-Chat, with the harmfulness classifier plus refusal matching as judge
relationships.reason: ASR is 0.75-0.99 on AdvBench (r1-r4) and 0.74-0.94 on the DeepInception set (r8-r9), so suffixes defeat refusal on the safety-trained models.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success was 0.75–0.99 on AdvBench and 0.74–0.94 on the DeepInception set.

relationships.condition: LLaMA2-7B-Chat, the most strongly aligned target, and GCG comparisons
relationships.reason: ECLIPSE reaches only 0.75 on LLaMA2, and GCG reaches 0.12 on LLaMA2 and 0.21 on Falcon (r5, r7). Success depends on the attack method and the target.
relationships.display_finding: ECLIPSE reached only 0.75 on LLaMA2, and GCG reached 0.12 on LLaMA2 and 0.21 on Falcon.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ECLIPSE suffix attacks on the tested models and datasets
reader_labels.reason: Reported ASRs range from 0.74 to 0.99 across ECLIPSE conditions, showing that suffixes can elicit harmful responses; see r1-r4 and r8-r9.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
